analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "We will hear arguments first this morning in the United States against Galliotto. Mr. Rotsfield, you may proceed whenever you are ready. Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court, this case concerns the constitutionality of a central provision of the federal gun control laws, the provision that keeps firearms out of the hands of people with a demonstrated history of mental illness. In those laws, in particular in Title IV, the Omnibus Crime Control and Safe Streets Act of 1968, and Title VII of the Gun Control Act of 1968, Congress chose to attack the problem of violent crime by prohibiting certain categories of what this Court has termed presumptively dangerous or especially risky people from acquiring guns. For people in some of these categories, such as fugitives from justice and aliens illegally present in the United States, this firearms disqualification remains in effect for as long as the person remains in the presumptively dangerous category. For the other groups of risky people identified by Titles IV and VII, the firearms disqualification is permanent. The only exception to this blanket rule involves a presumptively less dangerous subcategory of felons whose crimes did not involve the use of a firearm or other weapon. Someone in that group can obtain relief from the firearms disqualification if he is able to establish that he would not be likely to act in a manner dangerous to public safety. The events giving rise to this case that ultimately implicated these thigh arms disqualifications began in 1971 when the appellee voluntarily entered a psychiatric hospital. Shortly thereafter, he was involuntarily committed after suffering what was described as an acute mental breakdown, a condition that was diagnosed as an acute schizophrenic episode with paranoid features. He ultimately was released from the hospital after a stay of little more than three weeks, the time he was given a course of antipsychotic drugs advised to continue outpatient therapy. In 1982, Appellee tried to buy a gun from a federally licensed firearms dealer. The dealer refused to complete the sale after Appellee acknowledged on a standard Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, and Firearms form that he had once been committed to a mental institution. When Appellee then sought relief from BATF, he was informed that his prior commitment subjected him to a permanent federal firearms disqualification that could not be waived by the agency. The Appellee responded by bringing this suit in district court, claiming that the firearms disqualification is created by the gun control statutes, violated his Fifth Amendment rights to equal protection and due process. The district court agreed with the Appellee on both counts. The court concluded in lengthy dictum that former mental patients are a quasi-suspect class for equal protection analysis. The court went on to hold that Title IV is entirely irrational because it makes relief available to some felons, but not to people with a history of mental illness. The court also went on in alternative holding to conclude that Title IV makes use of an unconstitutional, irrebuttable presumption because it does not make provision for people who have been committed in the past to prove that they are no longer dangerous. As a result of these conclusions, the court invalidated all of the provisions of Title IV that create firearms disqualifications on the basis of mental disorder, a conclusion that apparently permits current as well as past psychiatric patients to obtain firearms. This court has addressed these firearms disqualifications on a number of occasions, and each time it has emphasized that Congress legislated as broadly as possible because it believes that only sweeping disqualifications would be effective in keeping guns away from dangerous people. The district court ignored that congressional understanding in holding, essentially, that Title IV is unconstitutional because it is insufficiently precise. Whether this holding was correct requires consideration of two questions. The first is whether Congress acted irrationally as an initial matter in listing people in the history of mental illness among the presumptively dangerous categories of people who are affected by the firearms disqualifications. Assuming that Congress acted properly in doing that, the second question is whether it was nonetheless under some kind of constitutional obligation to create an exception to this prophylactic rule for people who claim that they can establish that they are no longer dangerous. In our view, the answer to both of these questions is plainly no. As to the first question, it is not really disputed here that Congress acted rationally in prohibiting people with a history of commitment from acquiring firearms. At least since this court's decisions in O'Connor v. Donaldson, Addington v. Texas, a history of commitment has involved a commitment decision based on clear and convincing evidence that the comitie posed a danger of some sort to himself or others. Even Apple's commitment here in 1971, which predated those decisions, required a conclusion both by his attending physician and by the staff of his medical institution that he posed a potential danger to himself, to others, or to property, as well, apparently, as a judicial finding that he was a threat to himself or to society. This is a core issue here, whether the statute is infirm because it didn't provide any kind of alternative for persons previously adjudged not only deficient. I think that that's correct, Your Honor. The District Court itself acknowledged that Congress acted rationally in using a history of mental illness as a trigger for Title IV's prophylactic rules. And as you suggest, it went off entirely on the proposition that no relief provision had been added to the statute. The appellee has suggested in his brief that it may have been irrational as an initial matter for Congress to have listed people in this category as a presumptive matter in Title IV. And I'm suggesting now, I think, that that is easily disposed of and, in fact, as you suggest, was not taken seriously by the District Court. Certainly, it is true that in light of the meaning of the commitment decision, Congress undoubtedly acts rationally in prohibiting people who have been committed or who are currently under an order of commitment from getting guns. And given the relatively low rates of cure of mental illness and the fallibility and uncertainty of psychiatric diagnosis and treatment, which this Court has repeatedly recognized, Congress could act justifiably, concluding that someone whose mental disorder rose to a level requiring commitment should, at least as a presumptive matter, as you suggest, not be entitled to acquire firearms. And that leads to the second, then, for the District Court, the more troubling question in this case, whether having created and permissibly created this broad prophylactic rule, Congress was constitutionally obligated to carve out exceptions for people who believe that the rule is unfair as applied to them. That belief falls into that category. And that is what the District Court concluded. It felt that there was such a constitutional obligation on Congress. Now, in reaching that conclusion, the Court focused on 18 U.S.C. Section 925C, which is the provision that makes relief for the permanent firearms disqualification available to the less dangerous group of felons. The Court decided that it was entirely irrational for Congress to make relief available to any subcategory of felons while withholding it from people with a history of mental illness. Suppose the process by which he had been declared mentally disturbed had been modified and repudiated. Would he be able to get a license under this statute? Well, I think not, Your Honor. In fact, the commitment procedure in New Jersey has changed since the time of the appellee's commitment, and this Court has recognized additional constitutional requirements since then. But I think Congress could justifiably rely on a type of commitment procedure that, for example, is applied to the appellee here in determining that it gave some presumption of dangerousness to the person who was committed. It necessarily involved, even a flawed commitment proceeding involved, a finding by a judicial officer that the person who had been committed posed the danger to himself or to others. And that is the type of a factor that Congress is certainly entitled to taking into account and deciding who should have access to firearms. I mean, the district court's focus here was not really on the nature of the commitment decision where the procedures that were used by New Jersey, but on the fact that the federal statute provides relief to one subgroup of people affected by the disqualification and not to others, not people with the history of mental illness. And the Court decided that that must have been based on a stereotypical and inaccurate notion that mental illness is always incurable in every case. But this sort of analysis by the district court simply ignored the actual congressional intent in creating firearms disqualifications, as well as the unique factual characteristics of the mentally ill that set them apart from the other groups of presumptively dangerous people listed in Titles IV and VII. The Court failed to recognize that this Section 925C, the relief provision, this very narrow provision, withholds relief entirely from more dangerous felons who have used weapons during the commission of their crime. It also makes relief completely unavailable to all of the other especially risky categories affected by the Gun Control Acts, not only comitees and former comitees, such as the Apple II, but people who have been dishonorably discharged from the armed services, people who have renounced their American citizenship. Congress obviously recognized that everyone in each of these categories would not misuse a firearm were he able to obtain one. Mr. Rothfeld, is legislation pending presently in Congress to change this scheme somewhat? There are now three bills pending in Congress, Justice O'Connor, one of which has passed the Senate and another one of which has been reported out by the House Judiciary Committee, which would modify Section 925C. With respect to former mental patients? Yes, it would make relief available not only to former mental patients, but to all of the people subject to firearms disqualification. I mean, Congress has not as yet taken final action on that, and the bills differ as to their retroactive effect as well. But we'll inform the Court if there are further developments legislatively. In fact, the point that you bring up, that Section 925C is being considered now by Congress, suggests one of the flaws in what the District Court did. Congress 925C was originally enacted as a narrow response to a very specific problem faced by corporate firearms manufacturers who would be forced out of business altogether if they had been convicted of a felony, even one unrelated to their firearms operations. And after several years of experience with that narrow provision, Congress expanded it to benefit a larger but still a very small subcategory of felons. And that is the sort of legislation, one step at a time, that this Court has repeatedly upheld against equal protection challenges. The fact that Congress stopped, at least to this point, after fixing a defect that it saw in a felony disqualification, doesn't render the rest of Titles IV and VII unconstitutional any more than Congress has failed to list every imaginable group of presumptively dangerous people. in Titles IV and VII, when it initially passed them, renders invalid the very reasonable restrictions that it did create. And again, the fact that Congress is currently considering additional modifications of the 925C that would provide the appellee with all of the relief that he is currently seeking in court, it confirms that this sort of line drawing is a quintessentially legislative process that the District Court should not have involved itself in. But the statute is a permanent bar to the acquisition of guns by anybody who's been hospitalized for mental illness. That's correct. At the moment, anyone who has been involuntarily committed for mental illness. And the District Court, I take it, invalidated that entire disqualification? The District Court's, the relief that was provided by the District Court and the District Court is a little bit ambiguous. The Court concluded that it didn't have the authority to simply order BATF to create some sort of administrative mechanism that would allow someone such as appellee to prove that he is no longer dangerous. The Court decided it simply had to invalidate the provisions that regulate on it, that create disqualifications on the basis of mental disorder. And it therefore, in turn, struck down all the provisions in the District Court's words that prevent the appellee from purchasing a firearm. Do you think some narrower relief could have been provided? We suggest in our brief, Justice White, that, of course, the Court doesn't have to reach the question unless it concludes that there was a constitutional violation. But if it does, our view is that the relief that was granted was grossly out of proportion to the constitutional violation that the Court found. I mean, as a matter of equal protection, I think the Court, this Court's case has shown clearly that the proper remedy would have been either to extend the relief provision to people in appellee's category or to foreclose relief altogether for all people who are subject to firearms disqualifications. And even as a matter of due process, the Court also found a due process violation, is what clearly would have been the congressional intent that the presumptions, the disqualifications created by Title IV are not being validated altogether. And I think in that sort of situation that the remedy chosen by the District Court was inappropriate. The Court should have should have attempted to impose a hearing requirement or something with a burden of proof on the person who wanted a gun to show that he was no longer dangerous or that he never was. There is currently such a provision in Section 925C for, as I say, this less dangerous category of felon. They must establish to the satisfaction of the Secretary of the Treasury that they would be capable of handling a gun in a manner not dangerous to the public and that it would otherwise be in public interest to waive the firearm disqualification. Since Congress has signaled its intent there, a type of procedure that it would have in mind, and since Congress felt so strongly that people who are, certainly who are currently under an order of commitment, and as a general matter, anyone who has been found dangerous... Did the government make this argument in the lower court that that would have been a more proper remedy? The government did not argue this in the district court, Justice Warren. And so the court thought it didn't have authority to do anything but what it did? That was the court's stated reason, and the court recognized that what it was doing was completely inconsistent with the congressional intent and the basic permissible statutory scheme, and since, in our view, the court was clearly wrong in that judgment about its power, if this court ever reaches the question to think it is clear that the chosen remedy is an inappropriate one. To return briefly to the other equally fundamental flaw in the court's equal protection analysis, which we hope convinces this court not to reach the remedy question, the court, even apart from the legislative background, the evolution of Section 925C, ignored the significant reasons for withholding administrative relief from people with the history of mental illness that are simply not applicable to felons. People who have been committed, by definition, at some point have been found as a factual matter to have posed some sort of threat to themselves or others, to have been incapable of acting in an entirely rational way. That is not true of all felons. It's particularly not of the subcategory who benefited by Section 925C. And mental illness is an involuntary condition whose causes and course are not well understood. While many mental patients undoubtedly are cured, determining that any given patient will not have a recurrence of mental disorder requires an exercise of fallible psychiatric diagnosis and notoriously unreliable psychiatric predictions about an individual long-term future dangerousness. And this problem is confounded by the fact, as this case illustrates, that cures often involve continuation of drug or other types of therapy which are voluntary. Given these factors, Congress could prudently conclude, as it did, that the state of psychiatry simply does not permit prediction of anything near certainty that a person who has been committed in the past will not again prove dangerous to himself or others in the future. And for what it is worth, I should add that the empirical data available supports this judgment. The suicide rates of people in the history of mental illness appear to be disproportionately high, and it is generally acknowledged that the arrest rates of people who have been committed and released to mental institutions are significantly higher than those of the general population. While the briefs explain that there is currently a controversy raging in the psychiatric community about the causes of these facts, these phenomena, the very existence of these differential rates and the conclusions of some researchers that mental illness correlates directly with a propensity for greater violence and gives Congress all the support it needed to support its judgment that people in the history of mental illness are a presumptively risky group. Now, in this situation where the category of people affected by the classification presents an identifiable risk to the public, where the success of the Congressional purpose requires the use of broad prophylactic rules, where any single mistake would have catastrophic consequences for the public, Congress was entitled to act with all the caution it deemed necessary in lifting firearms disqualifications. Does the, I take it when you want to buy a firearm you fill out a form? That's correct, Justice White. And do you inquire whether, from a person, whether he's currently suffering from a mental illness? I believe the form only inquires whether he has in the past been committed to a mental institution or adjudicated incompetent. So he could be very mentally ill and still get a gun? That's true. So you never ask him whether he's now under medical care for a mental illness? I believe that's correct. I think the type of prophylactic rule that Congress created here and similar to the felony provisions the Court interpreted new banner most recently, Congress was looking for something that was easily applied and that would be probative. And I think it concluded reasonably anyone who was, whose mental disorder was serious enough to affect his ability to use firearms would likely have been committed in the past or that that would at least be a valid indicator. I think if the Congress, as a matter of administrative convenience, probably found, would have found it extremely difficult to require people to self-evaluate to determine whether or not they are currently mentally ill and the various levels of mental illness that might require treatment. And commitment is a sufficiently serious one that requires a finding of dangerousness to himself, to others, to society. I suppose there are a lot of examples of people voluntarily committing themselves who may be just as ill as those who were involuntarily committed. Well, it's certainly true that the disqualifications in Titles IV and VII don't reach everyone in society who's dangerous and shouldn't be able to obtain a gun. But Congress was creating, I think, prophylactic rules that focused on the most dangerous groups who were easily identifiable. that included felons and the others that I mentioned then includes people who have been actually adjudicated incompetent or requiring commitment. I mean, I think the fact that Congress could have gone further certainly doesn't evaluate the most serious restrictions that it did create in response to the most serious problem faced by the public. In fact, these same factors also answer the District Court's due process analysis. The District Court found the Title IV irrational because it imposes a firearms disqualification in response to a commitment while refusing to lift the disqualification in response to psychiatric testimony that the individual who's been committed will not be dangerous in the future. But those two forms of psychiatric judgment are quite distinct. Commitment decision is not a simple predictive matter. Commitment is ordered by a judicial officer as an immediate response to the patient's demonstrated inability to function in society. in contrast, the sort of evidence that the appellee would rely on, the District Court would rely on to raise the disqualification is the unreviewed testimony of a psychiatrist involving a much more subjective and unreliable opinion about long-term future dangerousness. And that's the sort of thing Congress wanted to avoid by focusing with particularity on whether or not a commitment had been ordered. There was a reliable judicial determination. There was certainly nothing irrational in Congress as deciding that of those two forms of psychiatric judgment, commitment was by far the most reliable. I'm not sure whether you covered it or not. Does the legislative history show anything about consideration by Congress of the fact that psychiatric predictions about future dangerousness are considered in the profession at least inherently unreliable or at least very dubious? Did Congress spend any time focusing on that? To my knowledge there is nothing in the legislative history directly touching on that. There are comments in the legislative history expressing the concern of legislators about possible future instability of people who have been found mentally ill in the past. But as you say there is a considerable amount of psychiatric literature at the moment which has been acknowledged by the court in a number of opinions suggesting that predictions about long-term dangerousness at least as to any given individual are extremely unreliable. And I think the court can take notice of that and certainly that provides Congress with all the factual support that it needed to rationally create the disqualifications that it did based on commitment. Before I conclude I should add one final point. I had just one one question that's perhaps rather theoretical but on the one step at a time analysis I've always it's always kind of an interesting problem. Supposing Congress thought that it would be generally desirable to cut down the use of guns throughout society which of course would not be terribly unreasonable and decided to do it gradually and said that for the first year the past staff said people whose names begin with A through D may not buy guns and if this seems to progress next year we'll take a look at another segment of the alphabet. Do you suppose that would be constitutional? Well I should emphasize of course that that's not what we have here. But it might be this case if one thought the classes were really indistinguishable that's why I asked the question and you've argued to the contrary on that but Well I think if Congress had the
